notes.title: Pilot units — capacity and what it cost
notes.content:
3B and 4A. Both carried the pilot on top of normal load.

3B had both training rounds. 4A had one, because the second fell in a week we were three nurses short and I cancelled it. That was my call and it is the most likely explanation for why 4A's numbers are flat.

The staffing shortfall itself is not something a vendor needs, and it would give them a story about why their product looks worse than it is.

notes.title: Observation requests — process
notes.content:
Any external party observing in a clinical area needs: the unit's agreement, a clinical escort, and a consent process for anything recorded. Lead time two weeks minimum.

This is not negotiable for a research session and I have said so.

notes.title: Scheduling templates — what a change costs
notes.content:
A template change ripples through booked appointments for six weeks. Anything that alters clinical capacity goes to governance first.

Most people asking for a template change want an operational change and do not need the template touched at all.

notes.title: Throughput — Q1
notes.content: Both units within target. 3B slightly ahead. No throughput impact from the pilot either way, which is worth saying because it was the fear going in.

notes.title: Second training round — blocked on what
notes.content:
Needs four hours of clinician time on 4A. I do not have it until the staffing gap closes, which is a recruitment problem, not a scheduling one.

Naomi and Kenji both want the round done before the April gate. I understand why. I still do not have the hours.

notes.title: Bed management — daily
notes.content:
Twice-daily huddle. Predicted discharges against expected admissions.

Prediction accuracy is around 60%, which sounds bad and is roughly what everyone achieves. The 40% is why escalation beds exist.

notes.title: Escalation capacity
notes.content:
Twelve escalation beds across two areas, opened by an on-call director's decision.

Opened forty-one times this year. Each opening costs agency staffing, and the cost never appears against the decision that caused it.

notes.title: Clinic templates — utilisation
notes.content:
Average utilisation 84%. Target 90.

The gap is short-notice cancellations that cannot be refilled. Text reminders moved did-not-attend rates about three points and then stopped moving them.

notes.title: Agency spend
notes.content:
Running above plan, driven by nursing vacancies on two units.

Every month the conversation is about agency spend and every month the answer is recruitment, which is not something operations can fix in a month.

notes.title: Theatre scheduling — not mine but adjacent
notes.content:
Different team, and their utilisation drives my bed demand.

The two schedules are built independently, which is how you get a full theatre list and no beds to recover into.

notes.title: Winter planning
notes.content: Starts in June. Everyone treats it as a September problem and by September the staffing decisions that would have helped have already been made.

notes.title: Portering and transport
notes.content: Median wait for a portering job is 22 minutes. That number is in every discharge delay analysis and it is never the actual cause, but it is always cited.

notes.title: Outpatient did-not-attend
notes.content:
8.1% overall, higher in some specialties for reasons that correlate with deprivation rather than anything clinical.

Worth saying explicitly because the default reading is that patients are unreliable.

notes.title: Staff rostering system
notes.content:
Rosters built six weeks ahead. Anything within two weeks is a manual conversation.

That two-week window is where every training request, every meeting, and every observation session collides.

notes.title: Discharge lounge — utilisation
notes.content:
Opened last year. Under-used because ward staff do not trust it and send patients only when the ward is full.

A facility used only under pressure never builds the trust that would let it relieve pressure.

notes.title: Capacity planning — annual
notes.content:
Built from activity projections that arrive late and change after they arrive.

The plan is always wrong. The value is that everyone had the argument in advance rather than in the middle of a bad week.

notes.title: Clinic templates — the estate
notes.content: Eighty-four templates across the service lines. Roughly a third have not been reviewed since they were built.

notes.title: Did-not-attend rate
notes.content: 9.8%, worse in the deprived postcodes and worse for morning slots. Text reminders moved it two points and nothing has moved it since.

notes.title: Overbooking policy
notes.content: Some clinics overbook by two to absorb DNAs. When everyone attends, the clinic runs ninety minutes late and the complaint is about waiting, not about booking.

notes.title: Staffing establishment versus actual
notes.content: Running at 88% of establishment across the medical-surgical units. Recruitment is open on nine posts and has been for five months.

notes.title: Bank and agency spend
notes.content: Up nineteen per cent year on year, entirely explained by the vacancies. Finance treats it as an overspend; it is a recruitment problem wearing a finance costume.

notes.title: Room utilisation
notes.content: 64% against a 85% target. The gap is mostly clinics that block rooms and do not use them, which is a behaviour problem and not a scheduling one.

notes.title: Escort and observation policy
notes.content: Any external party in a clinical area needs unit agreement, a clinical escort, and a consent process for recording. Two weeks lead time and it is not negotiable.

notes.title: Winter capacity plan
notes.content: Escalation beds, discharge lounge hours, and the point at which elective work is cancelled. Written every August and used every January.

notes.title: Why I say no to training in a short week
notes.content: Four hours of clinician time when a unit is two staff down is four hours the floor does not have. The request is always reasonable and the answer is still no.

notes.title: Throughput reporting — what the numbers hide
notes.content: Unit-level averages hide the two days a month when everything falls over. Those two days are what staff remember and what the average erases.

notes.title: Patient flow meeting — daily
notes.content: 08:30, fifteen minutes, every day. It is the single most useful meeting in the organisation and the one most often skipped by people who need it.

notes.title: Job planning cycle
notes.content: Annual. Consultant job plans, session allocation, and the negotiation that comes with both.

todos.content: Everyone wants it. The hours do not exist until recruitment closes.
